modules.title: Mental model
modules.sub: Starts the spine: the grading problem an LLM judge solves.
modules.summary: You can't read 10,000 model outputs by hand, and exact-match scoring fails on open-ended text. An LLM-as-Judge grades outputs against a rubric at scale. This module frames why it exists before we open up how it works.
objectives: Explain why LLM-as-Judge exists: scoring open-ended output at scale.
State the core risk: a judge can be confidently wrong, so it must itself be validated.
Name one rubric criterion you could grade against for a real task.

blocks.title: What LLM-as-Judge is — and the problem it solves

spans.text: Before reading on, predict:
you have 10,000 chatbot answers and want to know which are "helpful." Why can't a simple string-match or keyword check tell you that?
When you build something with an
eval

loop, you constantly need to score outputs: is this summary accurate? is this answer helpful? For open-ended text there is no exact answer to match against, and reading every output by hand does not scale.
LLM-as-Judge
solves this: you use a second LLM to grade outputs against a written
rubric
, cheaply and at scale.
The mental model is simple. A judge takes three things in and returns one thing out:

items.text: In: the rubric (what "good" means), the model output to grade, and optionally a reference answer.
Out: a verdict — a score, a label, or a pick between two outputs — plus a short rationale.
The catch: the judge is itself an LLM, so it can be confidently wrong. A judge you have not validated is just an opinion.

blocks.analogy: An LLM judge is like a grading TA handed a rubric: fast and consistent on clear criteria, but you still spot-check their grades against the professor's before trusting the whole stack.

modules.title: Mechanism
modules.sub: Follows the model: how a single judge call actually runs.
modules.summary: Now that you know why judges exist, open up one judge call: a rubric and an output go into a prompt, the LLM returns a verdict, and you parse a score out. This module traces those moving parts end to end.
objectives: Trace the four parts of a judge call: rubric, inputs, prompt, parsed verdict.
Explain why the judge must return structured output, not free prose.
Identify where in the call the score is produced and where it can drift.

blocks.title: The four parts of one judge call

spans.text: A
judge
is not magic — it is one structured LLM call. Every call has the same four parts, in order:

items.text: Rubric
— the written criteria for "good," baked into the system prompt (e.g. "score 1–5 on factual accuracy against the reference").
Inputs
— the output being graded, plus optionally a reference answer and the original question.
Prompt
— rubric and inputs assembled into one message that asks the judge model for a verdict and a rationale.
Parsed verdict
— you extract a structured score or label from the reply. This is where you record the result for the
eval
run.

spans.text: Ask the judge for structured output (JSON with a score field), not free prose. Prose is unparseable at scale and lets the score drift mid-sentence.

blocks.analogy: It's an assembly line: rubric defines the spec, the output is the part on the belt, the prompt is the inspector's checklist, and the parsed verdict is the pass/fail stamp.

blocks.title: Walk one judge call: grading a summary

spans.text: "Score the summary 1–5 on faithfulness to the source. 5 = no claims unsupported by the source; 1 = mostly fabricated." Write it once; reuse it for every output.
Pass the source document and the candidate summary. Faithfulness needs the source as a reference, so include it — without it the judge has nothing to check claims against.
The judge returns
{"score": 2, "rationale": "claims a 2024 date the source never states"}
. Parse the score; keep the rationale so a human can audit disputed grades later.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: pointwise vs pairwise

spans.text: Two outputs of the same mechanism. Pointwise: the judge scores one answer in isolation against the rubric ("rate this answer 1–5"). Pairwise: the judge sees two answers and picks the better one ("which response is more helpful, A or B?").
Pairwise is usually more reliable, because relative judgments are easier than absolute ones — but it costs more calls and only ranks, it does not give you an absolute quality number.

blocks.title: Technical note: log the rationale, not just the score

spans.text: Record every judge call as a
trace
: the rubric version, the inputs, the raw reply, and the parsed score. When a grade looks wrong, the rationale is what lets you tell a judge error from a real model failure.
Pin the judge model and temperature. A judge run at temperature 0 with a fixed model is reproducible; bump either and last week's scores stop being comparable.

blocks.prompt: Why should a judge return a structured score (e.g. JSON) rather than a free-text paragraph?

options.text: Because JSON is the only format LLMs can produce.
Because a structured score is reliably parseable at scale and pins the verdict to a field instead of letting it drift through prose.
Because free text always costs more tokens than JSON.

blocks.explanation: You run a judge over thousands of outputs. A score field can be parsed and aggregated deterministically; prose has to be re-interpreted and can contradict itself within the same reply.

modules.title: Design choices
modules.sub: Follows the mechanism: the calls that decide whether the judge is trustworthy.
modules.summary: The mechanism is fixed; the design is where quality is won or lost. Here you choose the scoring scale, whether to give the judge a reference, and pointwise vs pairwise — each trades reliability against cost.
objectives: Choose a scoring scale and justify it against rubric clarity.
Decide when a reference answer is required vs optional.
Pick pointwise vs pairwise scoring for a given goal.

spans.text: Quick recall from module 2:
what were the four parts of a single
judge
call? Try to name them before reading on.
(Rubric, inputs, prompt, parsed verdict.) The design choices below all live inside the rubric and inputs — they change what you feed the call, not its shape.

blocks.title: The three design choices that move reliability

spans.text: Three choices decide whether your
judge
is trustworthy. None has a universal right answer — each is a tradeoff.

items.text: Scoring scale.
Binary (pass/fail) is robust and easy to validate; a 1–5 scale is more informative but judges anchor and cluster scores in the middle.
Reference answer.
A gold reference makes grading far more reliable (the judge checks against a known-good answer) but requires you to author references — expensive, and impossible for truly open-ended tasks.
Pointwise vs pairwise.
Pairwise comparison is more reliable but only ranks; pointwise gives an absolute number you can track over time.

spans.text: Before reading on, predict:
if a 1–5 judge keeps returning 3 and 4 for everything, which design choice would you change first?

blocks.analogy: Like designing a survey: yes/no questions are easy to tally but lose nuance; a 1–5 Likert scale captures nuance but everyone hugs the middle. Same tradeoff, same fix — anchor the scale with concrete examples.

blocks.title: Which scoring design for your judge?

options.name: Binary pointwise (pass/fail)

cells.text: Highest — a clear threshold is easy for a judge to apply consistently.
Low — you only learn pass or fail, not how good or bad.

options.whenToUse: Use when the rubric has a crisp acceptance bar (e.g. "is it factually correct, yes or no?").

options.name: 1–5 pointwise scale

cells.text: Medium — judges anchor and cluster mid-scale unless you give per-point examples.
High — gives a tracked quality number over time.

options.whenToUse: Use when you need a trend line and can anchor each point with a concrete example.

options.name: Pairwise comparison

cells.text: High — relative judgments are easier than absolute ones.
Medium — ranks A vs B but gives no absolute quality level.
Many calls — every pair, and you may swap order to cancel position bias.

options.whenToUse: Use when comparing two systems or prompt versions head-to-head.

blocks.howToRead: Pick the smallest-cost option whose reliability and information meet your goal: binary for a clear bar, 1–5 for a trend, pairwise for head-to-head A/B.

blocks.title: Technical note: anchor the scale to beat mid-clustering

spans.text: If a 1–5 judge clusters at 3 and 4, the fix is rarely a bigger model — it is a clearer
rubric
. Give the judge a concrete example for each point on the scale and tell it to pick the closest match.
Also randomize the order of A and B in pairwise judging. Judges have a measurable position bias — they favor whichever answer comes first — and swapping order across runs cancels it.

blocks.prompt: You need an absolute quality number you can plot week over week. Which scoring design fits best?

options.text: Pairwise comparison, because it is the most reliable.
A 1–5 pointwise scale, because pairwise only ranks and gives no absolute level to track.
Whichever uses the largest judge model.

blocks.explanation: Pairwise tells you A beat B but not how good either is, so it can't be plotted as an absolute trend. A pointwise scale yields the number you can track over time.

modules.decisionItForces: Choose the judge's scoring design: binary pass/fail, a 1–5 pointwise scale, or pairwise comparison.

modules.title: Tiny implementation sketch
modules.sub: Follows the design: turn the chosen design into a minimal judge function.
modules.summary: Now write it. A judge is a small function: build the rubric prompt, call the model, parse a structured score. We start from a worked sketch, then you complete the parsing line — and check the AI-generated version before trusting it.
objectives: Write a minimal judge function: prompt in, parsed score out.
Complete the score-parsing step from a partial sketch.
Verify an AI-generated judge against a known-bad case before trusting it.

blocks.title: The shape of a judge function

spans.text: Every
judge
function — in any language — has the same three steps mapped straight from the mechanism in module 2:

items.text: Build the prompt
: insert the
rubric
, the output to grade, and any reference into a template that asks for JSON.
Call the model
at temperature 0 with a pinned judge model so runs are reproducible.
Parse the verdict
: pull the score out of the reply and fail loudly if it is missing or out of range.

blocks.analogy: It's the same shape as a unit test: arrange the inputs, run the thing under test, assert on the result — except the 'assertion' is an LLM applying a rubric.

spans.text: If you let an AI assistant generate a judge for you, verify it before trusting a single score:

items.text: Feed it a known-bad output. A judge that scores a deliberately wrong answer as "good" is broken — this is the fastest smoke test.
Check the parser handles a malformed reply (missing score field) without silently defaulting to 0 or 5.
Confirm temperature is 0 and the model is pinned, or your scores aren't reproducible.
Confirm the rubric is in the prompt verbatim — assistants love to paraphrase it into something vaguer.

blocks.title: A minimal judge function (completion problem)
blocks.code:
RUBRIC = "Score the answer 1-5 for factual accuracy vs the reference. Reply ONLY as JSON: {\"score\": int, \"rationale\": str}."

def judge(answer, reference):
    prompt = f"{RUBRIC}\n\nREFERENCE:\n{reference}\n\nANSWER:\n{answer}"
    reply = call_llm(prompt, model="judge-v1", temperature=0)
    verdict = json.loads(reply)
    score = verdict["score"]
    if not 1 <= score <= 5:          # fail loud on out-of-range scores
        raise ValueError(f"score {score} outside 1-5")
    return score, verdict["rationale"]

spans.text: The rubric is pinned in the prompt and demands JSON. The
temperature=0
call makes the score reproducible, and the range check turns a malformed verdict into a loud error instead of a silently wrong number.

predictThenReveal.prompt: The range check raises on a score outside 1–5. Before reading the next line: why fail loudly here instead of clamping the value to the nearest valid score (e.g. forcing a 7 down to 5)?
predictThenReveal.answer: An out-of-range score means the judge didn't follow the rubric — clamping hides that and pollutes your eval with a fabricated 5. Failing loud surfaces a broken judge prompt so you fix the cause, not the symptom.

syntax.explains: Parses the model's JSON reply into a dict so you can read the score field.
Makes the judge deterministic so the same input yields the same score.
Fails loudly when the verdict is out of range, instead of recording a bad score.

blocks.prompt: Why does the judge function call the model with temperature=0?

options.text: To make the judge cheaper to run.
So the same input yields the same score — scores stay reproducible and comparable across runs.
Because judges cannot run at any other temperature.

blocks.explanation: A non-zero temperature makes the judge stochastic, so the same output could score 3 one run and 4 the next. Temperature 0 pins the verdict, which is what lets you compare today's eval to last week's.

modules.summary: A judge you haven't validated is just an opinion. This module covers how judges break in practice — bias, mid-clustering, gaming — and the one check that makes a judge trustworthy: agreement with human labels on a held-out set.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: Why does LLM-as-Judge exist as a technique in the first place?

options.text: LLMs are always more accurate than humans at scoring text.
It lets you score open-ended outputs at scale without requiring a human to review every response.
It eliminates the need for any rubric or evaluation criteria.
It is only useful when you have a reference answer to compare against.

questions.explanation: LLM-as-Judge exists specifically to handle the scale problem: human review of every open-ended output is too slow and expensive, so a judge model automates scoring.

questions.prompt: Without looking back at the lesson: name the four parts that make up a single LLM judge call, in order.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Rubric (the criteria to score against), inputs (the prompt and/or response being judged), the judge prompt (which packages rubric + inputs into an instruction), and the parsed verdict (the structured score extracted from the model's output).
questions.explanation: Every judge call has these four parts: rubric → inputs → judge prompt → parsed verdict. Missing or blurring any one of them is where scoring drift typically enters.

questions.prompt: You are evaluating customer-support replies and need to compare two model variants to decide which one to ship. Which scoring approach fits best, and why?

options.text: Pointwise 1–5 scale, because it gives an absolute quality score for each reply independently.
Pairwise comparison, because directly ranking two replies against each other is more reliable for a head-to-head decision.
Binary pass/fail, because it is the simplest scale and easiest to parse.
No rubric is needed — just ask the judge which reply it prefers in free prose.

questions.explanation: Pairwise scoring is the right tool when the goal is a head-to-head decision between two variants; it sidesteps the calibration problems of absolute scales for relative comparisons.

questions.prompt: You ship a judge to production and notice it gives high scores to confidently-worded but factually wrong answers. Which failure mode best describes this?

options.text: Score parsing error — the verdict is not being extracted correctly from the model output.
Rubric ambiguity — the scoring criteria are too vague to distinguish good from bad answers.
Sycophancy / style bias — the judge rewards confident tone rather than actual correctness.
Reference answer drift — the judge is comparing against an outdated gold answer.

questions.explanation: Rewarding confident-sounding but wrong answers is a classic sycophancy/style-bias failure: the judge latches onto surface features (tone, fluency) instead of the rubric criterion of factual accuracy.

questions.prompt: Before relying on your judge in a real pipeline, what is the minimum validation step you should complete?

options.text: Run the judge on 1 million examples to average out any noise.
Measure the judge's agreement with human labels on a representative sample, and test it against at least one known-bad case.
Ask a second LLM to review the first judge's scores.
Confirm the judge returns structured output — that alone is sufficient for production readiness.

questions.explanation: Validation requires checking agreement with human labels (so you know the judge tracks what humans care about) and probing it with a known-bad case (so you know it can actually catch failures).
